summary: ACME is the protocol used to automatically get certificates for domain names. This document describes how a client can ask for a certificate for a subdomain. It also lets the client prove control of a parent domain, and a certification authority may then issue the subdomain certificate without a separate proof for that exact name, if its policy allows.

eli5.summary: If you can prove you own a whole house, a guard may let you into any room without checking each door. This lets the certificate checker trust you for rooms inside a domain you already proved.

questions: get certificate for subdomain without validating it
what is the acme ancestordomain field
subtitle: How an ACME client can prove control of a parent domain and get certificates for subdomains under it.

tldr.problem: ACME normally asks the client to pass a challenge for every domain name in a certificate. For many subdomains under a domain you already control, that is repeated work.
tldr.mechanism: The client proves control of an ancestor domain, and the server, if its policy allows, issues certificates for subdomains without a separate challenge. New fields let the client and server say so: subdomainAuthAllowed and ancestorDomain.
tldr.outcome: Whether subdomain issuance is allowed stays a matter of CA policy, which the RFC leaves out of scope. It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 9444 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2023 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It builds on RFC 8555 and leaves the decision to issue subdomain certificates to each server's policy.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
ACME (RFC 8555) lets a certification authority (CA), acting as the ACME server, and an applicant, acting as the ACME client, automate domain ownership validation and certificate issuance.

RFC 9444 describes how ACME can issue subdomain certificates without making the client fulfill an ownership challenge against the subdomain itself. The client only needs to fulfill a challenge against an ancestor domain.
sections.eli5: Proving you own the whole street can be enough to get keys to each house on it. This document explains how to ask for that.

sections.title: Subdomains and Ancestor Domains
sections.content:
The RFC tightens the meaning of subdomain. A domain is a subdomain of a different domain if it is contained within it, and a domain is never a subdomain of itself. An ancestor domain is a domain that contains the subdomain and has fewer labels. For nnn.mmm.example.com, both mmm.example.com and example.com are ancestors.

Comparisons are done on whole labels. So ooo.example.com is not a subdomain of oo.example.com. The security section repeats this: implementations must compare entire labels and not rely on a string prefix match.
sections.eli5: Names are like a family tree, and you compare whole words, not letters. Being a cousin named Joe does not make you a child of Joey.

sections.title: The Normal ACME Workflow
sections.content:
A typical ACME issuance has seven steps. The client POSTs a newOrder request with a set of identifiers. The server replies with an order object holding links to authorization objects and a finalize URI. The client fetches the authorizations with POST-as-GET requests and completes one of the listed challenges, for example by publishing a DNS TXT record. It then POSTs a CSR to the finalize API, learns the certificate URI from the updated order, and downloads the certificate.

The RFC notes that ACME does not require the identifier in a newOrder request to match the identifier in the authorization objects. Server policy dictates which authorizations are needed. This gap is what makes subdomain issuance possible without changing the core protocol. The only identifier type in the base document is dns, and this RFC is relevant only to that type.
sections.eli5: Normally you ask for a certificate, get a task to prove who you are, do the task, then collect your certificate. The server does not have to make the task about the exact same name you asked for.

sections.title: The subdomainAuthAllowed Field
sections.content:
The server uses a new optional boolean, subdomainAuthAllowed, in an authorization object. When present it MUST be true for authorizations where server policy allows certificates for any subdomain subordinate to the domain in the authorization. If it is missing, the default is false.

The same name is also used in two other places. In the identifier object of a newAuthz request, the client sets it to ask for a subdomain authorization. In the ACME directory metadata, a server can include it with the value true to advertise support for subdomain authorization, with a default of false.

If policy allows wildcard identifiers under the authorization, the server SHOULD also include the wildcard field with the value true, as RFC 8555 describes.
sections.eli5: It is a little flag on your pass that says, this one also covers the rooms inside. If the flag is missing, it only covers the one door.

sections.title: Pre-authorization and New Orders
sections.content:
With pre-authorization, a client authorizes a domain once, outside any specific order, then places several newOrder requests for identifiers in its subdomains. The client includes subdomainAuthAllowed in the identifier object of its newAuthz request. If the server is willing, it creates an authorization object that includes the flag set to true. If policy forbids it, the server can still create an ordinary authorization and MAY include the flag set to false.

For a normal order, the client can add an optional ancestorDomain string to the identifier. It names an ancestor domain against which the client MUST be able to fulfill a challenge. For example, an order for foo.bar.example.org with ancestorDomain set to example.org lets the server choose to issue a challenge against foo.bar.example.org, bar.example.org or example.org. A client that cannot fulfill challenges against an ancestor should leave the field out.

If the server accepts subdomain authorization for that ancestor, it creates the authorization against the ancestor and sets the flag to true. Otherwise it creates an authorization for the requested identifier and SHOULD NOT include the flag.
sections.eli5: You can show your ID once at the front desk and get a pass for later visits. Or you can tell the guard at the door which bigger place you could prove you own, and let the guard choose which proof to ask for.

sections.title: An Illustrative Call Flow
sections.content:
The RFC walks through a pre-authorization using DNS-based proof. In step 1 the client sends a newAuthz request for example.org with subdomainAuthAllowed set to true. The server returns a pending authorization offering a dns-01 challenge. The client publishes a DNS TXT record, posts to the challenge resource, and the server validates it and marks the authorization valid. The client then deletes the TXT record.

In steps 2 and 3 the client places orders for sub1.example.org and sub2.example.org. It does not need the flag again. Because a valid authorization already exists for the ancestor, the server returns an order with status ready, and the client finalizes it with a CSR and downloads the certificate.

If validation takes time, the server may answer the challenge with status processing and the client polls the authorization resource.
sections.eli5: You prove you own the building once. After that, each time you ask for a key to a new room, the desk just hands it over.

sections.title: Security and Server Policy
sections.content:
ACME for Subdomains keeps the same two goals as ACME: only an entity that controls an identifier can get an authorization for it, and an account key's authorizations cannot be improperly used by another account. It changes nothing about account key management, the ACME channel or validation channels, so the ACME security considerations still apply.

The one new assumption is that control over a domain may imply control over its subdomains. The RFC says this is safe in many ecosystems, since control of the domain can often be used to demonstrate control of subdomains anyway. In ecosystems where that is not true, a more complicated threat analysis and server policy might be needed. A client can deactivate an authorization or its whole account, for example after a key compromise.

Policy is explicitly out of scope. The RFC lists choices a server could make: allow subdomain issuance from ancestor proof, allow it only for certain ancestor domains, and allow DNS-based proof, HTTP-based proof or both. The CA policy checks in RFC 8555 still apply, such as whether the name is on the Public Suffix List.
sections.eli5: The guard still has rules. A building might say yes to owners of the whole building, only to some buildings, or only after certain kinds of proof. This document does not choose the rules.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA added subdomainAuthAllowed to two registries defined by RFC 8555. In the ACME Authorization Object Fields registry it is a boolean that is not configurable. In the ACME Directory Metadata Fields registry it is also a boolean. Both entries point to RFC 9444.
sections.eli5: The new flag was written into the official list of known ACME words so everyone spells it the same way.
